extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in U.S. First Amendment and constitutional law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize doctrinal criteria and categories used to evaluate when speech is protected or may be regulated under the U.S. First Amendment; cites leading tests and case law examples. Useful for readers seeking an overview of doctrines (obscenity, defamation, public-forum, content-based restrictions, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of First Amendment protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment applies to many expressions, including verbal and non-verbal communication, written communication, sign language, body language, facial expressions, gestures, symbols, and images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means that the First Amendment protects not just what we say but also how we express ourselves. (Page notes: the Amendment applies to verbal and non‑verbal communication, sign language, body language, facial expressions, gestures, symbols, and images.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unprotected speech — clear and present danger / imminent lawless action
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of speech are not protected, including speech creating a clear and present danger or that amounts to imminent lawless action (Brandenburg standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key cases cited include Schenck v. United States and Brandenburg v. Ohio; Brandenburg established the modern 'imminent lawless action' test (referenced at pages 447, 450).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation and false speech standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation (libel/slander) and false statements are subject to First Amendment doctrine and distinct standards depending on plaintiff status (e.g., public officials/public figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (actual malice standard for public officials) and Milkovich v. Lorain Journal Co. are cited; guidance revolves around whether statements are factual assertions, whether plaintiff is a public figure, and the actual malice requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fighting words and heckler's veto
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech consisting of 'fighting words' or that provokes a disproportionate hostile response may be unprotected; the 'heckler's veto' describes suppression based on audience reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited include Chaplinsky, Terminiello, Feiner, Gregory v. City of Chicago, Cohen v. California and others; doctrine evaluates whether the speech is likely to incite immediate breach of the peace or violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: True threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Threats that are 'true threats' are not protected speech and can be criminalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Virginia v. Black, Elonis v. United States, and Counterman v. Colorado are referenced; analysis distinguishes rhetorical hyperbole from actionable threats and considers speaker intent and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity and sexually explicit material
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscene material is not protected; courts apply multi‑part tests (e.g., Miller test) and have special rules for sexual materials involving minors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miller v. California establishes the Miller test for obscenity; New York v. Ferber and Osborne v. Ohio govern distribution of sexual material involving minors. The Constitution Annotated entry 'Amdt1.7.5.11 Obscenity' is cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech integral to criminal conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that is integral to criminal conduct can be regulated and is not protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York v. Ferber is cited as authority; the line between expression and actionable conduct is evaluated in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic speech versus conduct (expressive conduct tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions composed of conduct (symbolic speech) are evaluated under distinct tests to determine whether the conduct is protected expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases listed include Stromberg v. California, United States v. O'Brien, Cohen v. California, Spence v. Washington; O'Brien‑style balancing (government interest vs. expressive impact) often applies to regulation of conduct with expressive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content‑based restrictions (subject to strict scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions that are content‑based — i.e., that target speech because of its communicative content — are presumptively invalid and typically reviewed under strict scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key authorities referenced include Reed v. Town of Gilbert and many content‑based cases (e.g., Lamont, R.A.V., Simon & Schuster); strict scrutiny requires a compelling governmental interest and narrow tailoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content‑neutral restrictions (time, place, and manner / intermediate scrutiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content‑neutral regulations of the manner of expression are evaluated under intermediate scrutiny (time, place, and manner analysis) and may be upheld if they serve a significant government interest, are narrowly tailored, and leave open ample alternative channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited include Schneider, Renton, Clark; the doctrine distinguishes regulations aimed at non‑communicative aspects (noise, congestion) from content discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public forum doctrine (public, designated, nonpublic forums)
rubrics_metrics.description: The availability of governmental property for expressive activity is governed by forum classification: traditional public forum, designated public forum, and nonpublic forum — each permitting different degrees of regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In‑the‑public‑forum cases listed include Hague v. CIO, Thornhill, Martin v. Struthers, and many others; designated forum cases include Widmar v. Vincent, Rosenberger v. Univ. of Virginia, Uzuegbunam; nonpublic forum cases include Lehman v. Shaker Heights, Perry, Cornelius. The applicable standard depends on forum status (most protection in traditional public forums).

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated public forum
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government intentionally opens property for expressive activity, that property becomes a designated public forum and is treated like a public forum for First Amendment purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/cases: Rosenberger v. Univ. of Virginia, Uzuegbunam v. Preczewski. Restrictions in such forums are judged with heightened scrutiny appropriate to open access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpublic forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Government property not traditionally open to public expression is a nonpublic forum and may be subject to reasonable, viewpoint‑neutral restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Lehman v. Shaker Heights, Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators' Association, and Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense Fund illustrate that regulations in nonpublic forums are upheld if they are reasonable and viewpoint neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelled speech and compelled subsidy of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment limits the government’s ability to compel individuals or entities to speak or to subsidize others' speech against their beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key authorities include West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (compelled speech), Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo, and cases on compelled subsidy such as Abood, Janus, and related union dues/compelled subsidy jurisprudence (Janus and others). National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra and 303 Creative LLC v. Elenis also appear in the citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial speech regulation (Central Hudson framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial speech (advertising and similar) receives First Amendment protection but may be regulated under an intermediate test assessing misleadingness and substantial government interests (e.g., Central Hudson test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases and discussions include Central Hudson, Zauderer, Virginia State Pharmacy Bd. v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council, and many commercial‑speech cases listed (e.g., Bigelow, Bates, Ohralik). Analysis focuses on whether speech is misleading/illegal and whether regulation materially advances government interest and is no more extensive than necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student (school) speech standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech by students in public schools is protected but subject to limitations based on the school context (e.g., substantial disruption, curricular control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tinker v. Des Moines (substantial disruption test), Bethel School District v. Fraser, Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier, Morse v. Frederick, Island Trees (Pico) and subsequent student‑speech cases define varying standards depending on whether speech is on‑campus, school‑sponsored, lewd, or causing disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public‑employee speech standards (Pickering/Garcetti/Connick)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech by public employees is evaluated under balancing frameworks that weigh employee speech interests against government employer interests and workplace efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key cases include Pickering v. Board of Education (balancing), Connick v. Myers (practical workplace considerations), Garcetti v. Ceballos (speech pursuant to official duties). The doctrine examines whether speech addresses matters of public concern and the impact on government operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overbreadth and vagueness doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws that are overbroad (sweep substantially protected speech) or vague (fail to give fair notice of prohibited conduct) can be struck down under the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases and doctrines cited include Terminiello, Smith v. Goguen, Board of Airport Commissioners v. Jews for Jesus. Courts invalidate statutes that chill protected expression or allow arbitrary enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government speech doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government itself is speaking, the First Amendment does not constrain the government in the same way it constrains regulation of private speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases include Pleasant Grove City v. Summum and Walker v. Texas Div., Sons of Confederate Veterans; doctrine distinguishes government‑sponsored messages from regulation of private speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and prior restraint / regulation of distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing schemes, prior restraints, and other regulatory systems governing distribution or access to speech are subject to heightened scrutiny and special doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities referenced include Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Comm'n of Ohio, Freedman v. Maryland, Murdock v. Pennsylvania, and many licensing cases; the focus is on procedural safeguards and the heavy presumption against prior restraint.
